slides.headline: The job token. In one sentence
slides.body: every job gets its own short-lived token for the repository that contains the workflow, and the permissions key decides what that token may do.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: The documentation: "At the start of each workflow job, GitHub automatically creates a unique GITHUB_TOKEN secret to use in your workflow."

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: What the token may do is decided in three layers.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: The repository or organization default: the setting called "Workflow permissions".

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: The workflow: the top-level permissions key sets the token of every job that doesn't override it.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: The job: a permissions key under the job sets the token of that job only.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: Three rules of the key carry most of the weight.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: Rule one, quoted: "If you specify the access for any of these permissions, all of those that are not specified are set to none."

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: Quick quiz. A workflow's only permissions line is issues: write.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: B. Naming one scope sets every other one to none, reading contents included.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: Rule two: permissions with an empty map removes everything.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: Rule three: the scopes. On the first of October 2026 the list has sixteen names, among them actions, attestations, checks, contents, deployments, id-token, issues, packages, pull-requests …

slides.caption: Older behavior: a workflow without a permissions key received a read-write token.
So the answer to "what can the token do when there is no permissions key?" is: it depends on a setting you can't see in the file …

slides.direction: The unsafe and the safe form, side by side.
slides.title: yaml

lines.s: # Unsafe: every job, and every action in every job, can push, tag, release and edit issues.
# Safe: read-only for the workflow; one job adds the one scope it needs.
issues: write        # contents is now none for this job, which is fine: it checks nothing out

slides.headline: Two properties limit what a stolen job token can do
slides.body: First: events triggered by the GITHUB_TOKEN will not create a new workflow run, with workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch as the documented exceptions.

slides.headline: Inside .git
slides.body: The token also reaches Git.

slides.headline: Inside .git
slides.body: Since version 6 of the action the credential is stored in a separate file under the runner's temporary directory.

slides.headline: Analogy for the model,
slides.body: from the textbook. A contractor is let into your office each time a parcel arrives.

slides.headline: Analogy for the model,
slides.body: Three things can go wrong. The badge opens too many doors.

slides.headline: Analogy for the model,
slides.body: The analogy breaks in one place that matters: this contractor executes text literally and instantly, so a label that contains an instruction is carried out before anyone can notice.

slides.headline: Analogy for the token
slides.body: A visitor badge printed at the start of each shift and shredded at the end.

slides.headline: Analogy for the token
slides.body: It breaks because every tool the visitor picks up can use the badge without asking.

slides.headline: Analogy for the token
slides.body: Put the two together and you have the reason for least privilege.
Try it now, thirty seconds, on paper.

slides.body: Open the repository's settings for Actions and find the setting the documentation calls "Workflow permissions".
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Relying on the default token permissions. Root cause: the default is a repository or organization setting, read-only only for repositories created since 2 February 2023; the file does not show it.

beats.text: The repository or organization default: the setting called "Workflow permissions". It decides what a workflow with no permissions key gets. There are two options, quoted from the documentation: "read and write access for all permissions", or read access for the contents and packages permissions only.

There are two options, quoted from the documentation: "read and write access for all permissions", or read access for the `contents` and `packages` permissions only.

beats.text: The workflow: the top-level permissions key sets the token of every job that doesn't override it.
beats.tele: The workflow: the top-level `permissions` key sets the token of every job that doesn't override it.

beats.text: The job: a permissions key under the job sets the token of that job only.
beats.tele: The job: a `permissions` key under the job sets the token of that job only.

beats.text: Three rules of the key carry most of the weight.
beats.tele: Three rules of the key carry most of the weight.

beats.text: Rule one, quoted: "If you specify the access for any of these permissions, all of those that are not specified are set to none." So writing contents: read also removes issues, packages, pull-requests and every other scope. A scope is one named area of access.

beats.text: Quick quiz. A workflow's only permissions line is issues: write. Can its token read the repository's contents? A, yes. B, no. Your answer?

beats.text: B. Naming one scope sets every other one to none, reading contents included. Almost everyone expects A the first time.

beats.text: Rule two: permissions with an empty map removes everything. read-all and write-all are the two shorthands.
beats.tele: Rule two: `permissions` with an empty map removes everything. `read-all` and `write-all` are the two shorthands.

beats.text: Rule three: the scopes. On the first of October 2026 the list has sixteen names, among them actions, attestations, checks, contents, deployments, id-token, issues, packages, pull-requests, security-events and statuses. Each takes read, write or none, and write includes read.
beats.tele: Rule three: the scopes. On the first of October 2026 the list has sixteen names, among them `actions`, `attestations`, `checks`, `contents`, `deployments`, `id-token`, `issues`, `packages`, `pull-requests`, `security-events` and `statuses`. Each takes `read`, `write` or `none`, and `write` includes `read`.

beats.text: Older behavior: a workflow without a permissions key received a read-write token. Current behavior: the default is read-only for new repositories, organizations and enterprises. Since the second of February 2023, and the changelog adds: "this change will not impact any existing enterprises, organizations or repositories". Recommended: never rely on the default. Declare permissions at the top of every workflow, because a repository created before February 2023 may still have the permissive setting. The Nx project's post-mortem, its published account of the incident, names exactly this as one of three causes.

beats.text: So the answer to "what can the token do when there is no permissions key?" is: it depends on a setting you can't see in the file, and on when the repository was created.

beats.text: Read the comment in the second block. The job-level block replaces the workflow-level one, so contents is none for that job. That's correct here, because the job checks nothing out. GitHub's guidance says the same in prose: set the default permission to read access only for repository contents, and increase it as required for individual jobs. That practice is called least privilege: the smallest set of rights that does the job.

beats.text: Two properties limit what a stolen job token can do. First: events triggered by the GITHUB_TOKEN will not create a new workflow run, with workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch as the documented exceptions. The textbook warns that the exception isn't academic: in the Nx incident a stolen read-write token was used to dispatch the publish workflow. Second: the token dies with the job.

The textbook warns that the exception isn't academic: in the Nx incident a stolen read-write token was used to dispatch the publish workflow. Second: the token dies with the job.

beats.text: Inside .git. The token also reaches Git. The checkout action, which fetches the repository onto the runner, says in its README: "The auth token is persisted in the local git config. This enables your scripts to run authenticated git commands. The token is removed during post-job cleanup. Set persist-credentials: false to opt-out."

beats.text: Since version 6 of the action the credential is stored in a separate file under the runner's temporary directory. Either way, until the job ends, every later step and every process it starts can run authenticated Git commands against your repository with whatever contents permission the job has. A job that only builds and tests has no reason to leave it there.

beats.text: Analogy for the model, from the textbook. A contractor is let into your office each time a parcel arrives. The front desk gives the contractor a badge, and the badge opens whatever doors the desk configured. The contractor follows a written procedure, which is the workflow file. Uses tools bought from other firms, which are actions. And reads the label on the parcel, which is event data.

beats.text: Three things can go wrong. The badge opens too many doors. The procedure was written by the person who sent the parcel. Or the contractor reads the label aloud as if it were an instruction.

beats.text: The analogy breaks in one place that matters: this contractor executes text literally and instantly, so a label that contains an instruction is carried out before anyone can notice.

beats.text: Analogy for the token. A visitor badge printed at the start of each shift and shredded at the end. The desk can print it with access to one room or to the whole building.

beats.text: It breaks because every tool the visitor picks up can use the badge without asking. The documentation: "An action can access the GITHUB_TOKEN through the github.token context even if the workflow does not explicitly pass the GITHUB_TOKEN to the action."

beats.text: The fix isn't to switch the new repository to the permissive option. It's to declare permissions: contents: read at the top of every workflow in both repositories, and to add the one write scope to the one job that creates the release. After that, the two repositories behave the same, and the files say what the tokens can do.
